newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister urges shift to hi-tech society.
newsitem.headline: German minister urges shift to hi-tech society.

text.p: Germany must make the leap from an industry- to a knowledge-based economy to compete in the global marketplace and fight record post-war unemployment, Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers said on Friday.
"I don't believe typical industries can achieve the growth which will create jobs," Ruettgers told reporters. "We must abandon old industrial thinking and become a society based on knowledge."
He was speaking after figures released on Thursday showed that German unemployment hit 4.16 million in December, on a seasonally adjusted basis, the highest since World War Two.
Although Germany's flashy cars, precision machine-tools and chemical products are all world beaters, those industries are shedding hundreds of thousands of workers.
Meanwhile, Germany lags in high-technology sectors like communications and electronics which should be the job-makers of the future, a report by Ruettgers' Research and Technology ministry found.
"Germany's position has hardly changed in the 1990s -- the car, machine and chemical sectors remain our strengths. But Germany is not specialised in leading technologies," it said.
Ruettgers said the jobs climate in Germany was "ambivalent" and warned that the ongoing economic recovery alone would not be sufficient to eat into unemployment levels as in past economic upturns.

Some economic forecasters say the official projection of 2.5 percent growth this year, reaffirmed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday, is too optimistic. They say Germany, with its high labour costs, faces a phase of so-called "jobless growth".
With increasing numbers of highly trained engineers and chemists finding themselves out of work, university science students are often giving up on looking for jobs in industry, Ruettgers said.
"I am convinced young people in Germany are not hostile to technology," Ruettgers said, warning "we will be desperately looking for engineers and chemists in five years."

Although the German government has made big efforts to clear away some of the regulatory tangle which hampers the emergence of new industries, a young generation of entrepreneurs has not yet sprung up.

"A structural shift in industry through founding new businesses is not enough to counter the weaknesses in the German economy. This deficit could have grave consequences over the medium term for growth and jobs," the report said.
